_comment: PUBLIC model constants only. Nothing here identifies a seat, a price paid, or an account. Anything personal - seat location, season invoice, tier credit amounts, list prices - lives in the user's browser profile and is never committed or served. See src/lib/profile.ts.

ticketmaster.label: Ticketmaster / NHL Ticket Exchange
ticketmaster.source: MEASURED at THREE independent price points, all exactly 0.9000: $77.00 -> $69.30, $70.00 -> $63.00 (two listings), and $85.00 -> $76.50 (two listings, with the fee itemised as -$8.50 per ticket = exactly 10%).
ticketmaster.openQuestion: RESOLVED 2026-09-05. Third-party sources cite 10-15%, but the rate is flat 10% across the two price points measured. The earlier corroboration (dividing instant offers by 0.9 yielding round dollars) was circular because it assumed 0.9; the $70 -> $63.00 observation is direct and independent of it. Still unmeasured: whether the rate holds at much higher prices, or differs by tier. Both $77 and $70 are low-priced listings on preseason inventory.
ticketmaster.whyItMatters: Break-even = credit / (1 - feeRate). At 10% an A+ break-even is credit/0.90; at 15% it is credit/0.85 - roughly 6% higher on every game. A systematic error here biases every pricing decision in the same direction.
ticketmaster.validationPlan: Largely done. To close the remaining gap, record 'You will make' at a materially higher list price (say $150+) on a regular-season tier.
ticketmaster.payoutNote: Deposited to a bank account typically within 5-7 BUSINESS days of the sale per the Edit Listing dialog, while the My Listings banner says 'typically within 7 days after the event'. Those are different clocks - business days from sale vs calendar days from the event - and which governs is unverified. Requires taxpayer/TIN info on file before any payout is released.

minListPriceRatioOfFace.source: Published Sharks365 variable-pricing FAQ: 'Sharks365 Members can post their tickets for resale up to 20% below the ticket price of the game selected for resale.' Worked example given: a $150.00 member rate implies a $120.00 minimum list.
minListPriceRatioOfFace._whyItMatters: A hard FLOOR on how far a listing can be marked down, which the model did not have at all. It binds precisely in the endgame the app currently describes as 'mark down aggressively': after the T-48h deadline you cannot list below 0.8 x face, so the worst a sale can net is 0.8 x face x 0.9 = 0.72 x face. If the market will not clear at that, the outcome is $0 rather than a smaller sale.
minListPriceRatioOfFace.openQuestion: The published rule governs Sharks365 member resale through Account Manager / TicketExchange. Whether Ticketmaster's general marketplace enforces the same floor on these listings is NOT verified - the measured $70 listings sat far above it, so the constraint has never been tested in practice.

listingCutoff.behaviour: an unsold listing is removed automatically at a configurable cutoff
listingCutoff.defaultObserved: puck drop (the dialog's prose) vs 2 hours after (the dropdown's stated default)
listingCutoff.source: Edit Listing dialog, 2026-09-05: prose read 'automatically removed on Tue Sep 22, 2026 07:00 PM' - puck drop - while the dropdown showed 'Tue Sep 22, 2026 09:00 PM (Default)'. The two disagree by two hours.
listingCutoff._whyItMatters: The model assumes an unsold listing simply expires worthless at puck drop. If listings are pulled EARLIER than puck drop, the window to sell is shorter than modelled, which matters in the endgame after the exchange floor is gone. Cheap to settle: read the dropdown's options.

exchange.label: Sharks Exchange (Return For Credit)
notes: CONFIRMED: an active listing can be delisted and then returned for credit. This is what makes 'list high, fall back to the credit' safe.
CONFIRMED: credit is a pure tier constant. Samples across different opponents, weekdays, and start times matched exactly within each tier.
Credit explicitly EXCLUDES any service fees previously paid on the tickets.
Credit lands as account credit, not cash - it only has value if it gets spent.
Hard deadline 48h before puck drop. After that the exchange floor is gone entirely.

CONFIRMED from published terms 2026-09-05: credit expires at puck drop of the last regular-season home game, does NOT roll over, and cannot buy playoff tickets. So the exchange floor shrinks through the season and does not exist at all for the final game.

creditHaircut._comment: Discounts account credit against cash. 1.0 would treat credit as good as money; 0.9 is Wesley's own valuation of it.
creditHaircut._resolved: The question this key was blocked on is ANSWERED (Wesley, 2026-09-05, plus the published terms in ops#30): credit does NOT roll into next season's renewal invoice and cannot buy playoffs. See creditSpendableOn.rollsOverToNextSeason=false and creditExpiry, both `measured`, in this same object. The escape hatch that would have made 1.0 defensible is closed, so 1.0 now OVERSTATES the credit for every game except those with many outlets remaining.
creditHaircut._effect: Break-even list price = credit * haircut / (1 - feeRate). At 0.9 every break-even drops ~10%, so the profitable listing band WIDENS and a sale becomes more attractive relative to the credit than it looked at 1.0. Concretely, preseason: break-even moves from credit/0.9 to credit*0.9/0.9.
creditHaircut._why09: ASSUMED, and it always will be - this is a preference, not a fact about the world, so no amount of collection settles it. What makes 0.9 better evidence than the 1.0 it replaces is simply that Wesley supplied it and 1.0 was a placeholder nobody chose. Recorded with his number rather than an agent's, because an agent picking 0.8 to look precise is the fabricated precision rule 4 forbids.
creditHaircut._whyNotLower: Credit is constrained - same season only, no playoffs, no rollover, and Wesley already holds a seat at every home game, so it buys only extras. That argues for a steeper discount than 0.9. He chose 0.9 anyway, which is his call to make and is consistent with actually spending it on upgrades or additional seats he wants. If outcomes later show credit going unspent at season end, that is evidence to revisit.
creditHaircut._notTheWholeStory: This is a flat discount and the decay is NOT folded into it. The structural part is modelled separately and does not depend on this number: remainingCreditOutlets() and exchangeIsRealFloor() in src/lib/economics.ts remove the floor entirely for the final home game. A game with few outlets left is worth less than 0.9 and the model does not yet say so - deliberately, because the shape of that decline has no evidence behind it. See ops#25.

creditExpiry.source: Published Sharks365 Ticket Exchange FAQ: 'Any unused account credit will expire at puck drop on the last game of the current season.'

creditSpendableOn.scope: regular season home games of the SAME season only
excluded: purchases on sjsharks.com, ticketmaster.com, or TicketExchange by Ticketmaster
creditSpendableOn._whyItMatters: This closes the escape hatch that would have made creditHaircut=1.0 defensible. Credit CANNOT be applied to next season's renewal invoice and CANNOT buy playoff tickets, so it must be spent on a remaining regular-season home game or it dies. Its value therefore DECAYS through the season and is effectively zero for the final home game - see creditDecay.

creditDecay._comment: Derived from the published expiry and spend scope, not from a fitted curve. Credit from returning game G can only buy tickets to a regular-season home game that has not happened yet. For the LAST home game (2027-04-10 vs ANA, tier A+) that set is empty apart from the game itself, so the credit's only use is buying different seats to the game you just returned - economically not an exit. That game therefore has NO exchange floor: its outcomes are 'it sells', the instant offer, or $0. The count of remaining games is MEASURED; how sharply value falls as that count shrinks is a preference (Wesley already holds a seat at every home game, so credit buys only extras) and is deliberately not modelled as a curve.
creditDecay.additionalFrictionNotModelled: The FAQ warns inventory is first-come first-served and some games may be unavailable, so spendability degrades as games sell out too - not only as games run out. Not modelled; it would be invented.

oneForOneExchange.source: Published FAQ: 'Ticket exchanges within the same tier and within the same price code will be a 1-for-1 exchange, meaning the net total of the transaction will be $0.'
oneForOneExchange._comment: A distinct exit from return-for-credit: move seats game-to-game within a tier at no cost. Not currently in the model's four exits.

instantOffer.label: Ticketmaster 'Sell Your Tickets Now' instant buyout
notes: SOLVED: the offer is a buyer's BID at a round dollar price, paid out net of the same 10% seller fee. FOUR samples, all exact:
CONSEQUENCE: the seller page leaks a live market price for free. No scraping needed for this number.
IMPORTANT: this is a BID, not an ask. It is a floor on market value, not fair value. A patient listing should clear above it - measuring that spread is a core job of the collector.
Ticketmaster states it does not set the offer amount.

OBSERVATION: in all four samples the implied bid net was BELOW the tier exchange credit, including for marquee A+ opponents. If that holds, the instant offer is never the right exit while the exchange window is open.
Only visible on the authenticated seller page, so this is manual-paste data, not scraped.

MEASURED 2026-09-05: raising the ask from $70 to $85 on both preseason games left the instant offers UNCHANGED ($24.30 and $27.90 per ticket). Consistent with the offer being a buyer's bid that does not respond to the seller's ask - which is what makes it a floor on value rather than a function of our pricing.
